title: Continuous Chain of Thought Enables Parallel Exploration
one_liner: Instead of picking one word at a time, a language model can generate soft blends of many words at once, letting it explore multiple reasoning paths in parallel.
lead: Language models normally think step by step by picking one word from a list and then the next word and so on. This paper asks: what if the model could generate a soft blend of many words at each step instead of just one? That blend gives the model room to track multiple reasoning branches at the same time, like exploring several paths through a maze without committing to one choice until the end.

problem.h2: Why picking one word at a time gets stuck
paras: A standard language model picks one word at each step and keeps going forward. If that choice was wrong, it is too late to change it; the path is locked in. A beginner might hope the model could explore multiple branches at once, but the normal word-picking process does not allow that because it forces a single commitment: you pick one discrete word (100% probability to that word, 0% to all others), feed it to the next step, and once it flows through the reasoning layer, that choice is locked in with no way to backtrack. Each step chooses one discrete word from the vocabulary, leaving no room to hold many possibilities in parallel.

Some reasoning problems require the model to track multiple branches simultaneously to avoid dead ends. Finding the minimum sum of a set of numbers is an example: you must consider many different combinations to find the best one. But a model that commits to one path at each step gets stuck exploring only one combination and misses the optimal answer.

callout.html: Standard models pick one word at each step, so they cannot explore multiple reasoning paths in parallel.

steps.text: Instead of picking one word, output fractions: 40% word A, 30% word B, 30% word C.
Use that blended representation as input to the next reasoning step.
All three paths flow through independently; each gets processed by the reading layer and the next layer.
Sample K top words from each soft blend, average their number-lists, and use that for the next step.
Train by showing the model many correct solutions and teaching it to match the average next-word choice.

paras: Normally the model outputs a single word at each step (100% to one, 0% to all others). This paper changes it to output a soft blend: different fractions spread across many words at once. That blended representation becomes the input to the next step.
object.object: Output: one word to soft blend

hidden.h2: Tracking parallelism: how many paths at once
hidden.name: Parallelism capacity (max branches per step)
paras: The paper measures a quantity called parallelism: how many different reasoning branches can the model hold in the soft blends at once? A soft blend at step 2 can represent multiple paths from step 1 only if the model has enough embedding dimension (the count of numbers used to represent each word). If the dimension is too small, the soft blends start to crush and mix together, and paths interfere.

The paper proves mathematically that the embedding dimension directly controls the maximum parallelism. More dimensions mean more branches. They show that a single-layer model with sine and cosine embeddings can pack all possible states of a search problem (like exploring all subsets in the subset-sum problem) if the dimension is large enough.

heat.caption: Darker means higher capacity. At dim 24, enough room for multiple branches to stay separate.

reads.html: The embedding dimension is how many numbers describe each soft blend. Bigger numbers give the model more room to hold separate branches without them crushing together.
The paper constructs a single-layer model where sine and cosine embeddings can store all 2^k reachable states at step k, provided the embedding dimension d is at least 2^k.

paras: When you blend word A, word B, and word C into one token, that token holds all three. The model's attention layer (the piece that reads earlier words) can extract from all three branches at once. Each branch flows forward independently, like water splitting through channels and then rejoining.

During training, the model learns which soft blend to output by watching many correct solution traces. Instead of teaching it to pick word A with probability 100%, the paper shows it many paths and teaches it to average the next-word choices across all of them. This anchors soft tokens in real solutions.

At inference, the model samples K words (like 5) from the soft blend and averages their numerical representations. This sampling keeps the soft token crisp while holding multiple paths. The averaged representation then feeds to the next step, which can branch again.

stages.s: Soft token holding fractions of word A, B, C
Attention reads all three branches at once
Each fraction evolves through the next reasoning layer
Sample K top words; average their number-lists
New soft token for next step; repeat

math.words: Minimize the difference between what the model outputs and the blended distribution of all target traces at each step.
math.equation: Loss = sum over steps t of divergence(output_distribution_t, target_blend_t)
symbols: The soft token the model produces at step t (fractions summing to 1)
The average of target distributions at step t across all correct paths
A measure of how different two distributions are (like distance between them)
Add up the error at every reasoning step

worked.title: Tiny worked example: learning to blend two paths
lines: Suppose at step 2, path A says the next word is apple (100%), and path B says banana (100%).
The target blend at step 2 is: 50% apple, 50% banana.
Divergence measures how far 60%/40% is from 50%/50%.
Loss = that divergence (plus losses from all other steps).

math.note: The model learns the right soft blend by watching many successful reasoning paths and averaging their next-word choices.

charts.title: Discrete one-word model
charts.note: Model gets stuck because it cannot hold multiple branches at once. Needs more layers to recover.

charts.title: Continuous soft-blend model
charts.note: Model holds all branches in soft tokens. One layer with large dimension solves the problem cleanly.

items.html: If the model does not have enough embedding capacity, different branches start to crush and interfere. The soft token becomes gibberish and paths mix together. The model needs dimension to scale with the number of branches.

items.b: Sampling too few words from the blend.
items.html: If you sample only 1 word instead of 5 or more, the soft token collapses back to discrete. You lose the parallelism benefit.
The supervision depends on having good example solutions to learn from. If all target paths are suboptimal, the model learns to blend garbage.
With enough embedding dimension, diverse target paths, and K-token sampling, the soft tokens preserve branch separation and solve reasoning problems efficiently.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small transformer and train it on the subset-sum problem: given a list of numbers (like 3, 7, 2, 5, 9), find the subset that sums to a target value (say, 15). This is a search problem where the model must explore multiple branches. Train one version with discrete (one-word) outputs and one with continuous (soft-blend) outputs. Both should use the same embedding dimension. Measure how many steps each needs and how often they find the right answer.
demo.metric_eq: Success rate = (times model found correct subset sum) / (total test cases)
demo.closing: The soft-blend model should find the answer with far fewer steps and higher accuracy because it holds multiple branches. The discrete model should get stuck on hard cases.
